Hungary’s OTP Bank is set to enter the Baltic banking market through the acquisition of Luminor Bank, according to a statement published on Luminor’s official website. The announcement said OTP Bank has signed an agreement to acquire Luminor from a consortium of private equity funds managed by US investment firm Blackstone and DNB Bank. The acquisition will expand OTP Bank’s presence to 14 countries, increase its total assets by more than 10%, and raise the share of its operations within the euro area to 50%, the statement said. OTP Bank said it intends to continue supporting Luminor’s growth by building on the bank’s existing strengths, market position and customer relationships. The OTP Group also plans to establish a long-term presence in the Baltic region and, through Luminor, contribute to the financial well-being of customers across the three Baltic states. According to the bank, the acquisition represents not only a geographical expansion but also “a strategic entry into a developed and stable region with significant growth potential.” OTP Bank Chairman and CEO Péter Csányi said the group’s objective is to further strengthen Luminor’s position in the Baltic states while supporting the development of the region’s financial system, lending activity and financial innovation. Luminor CEO Wojciech Sass said both banks share a strong commitment to serving customers, creating long-term value and financing local economic growth. He added that becoming part of OTP Group would provide Luminor with the backing of an experienced international banking group with a strong presence across Central and Eastern Europe. The acquisition remains subject to approval by financial regulators before it can be completed. According to Latvia’s LETA news agency archive, OTP Bank had already expressed interest in acquiring Luminor several years ago. At the time, the Hungarian banking group operated in Hungary as well as Albania, Bulgaria, Croatia, Moldova, Montenegro, Serbia, Slovenia, Ukraine and Uzbekistan, among other markets. In 2024, the Bank of Latvia said the proposed acquisition would be assessed by the Estonian financial supervisor together with the European Central Bank (ECB). Because Luminor is incorporated in Estonia, the approval process would include a comprehensive assessment of the prospective shareholder’s impact on the entire banking group, including its branches in Latvia and Lithuania. The Bank of Latvia noted that decisions on significant acquisitions are approved by the ECB’s Supervisory Board, where Latvia’s central bank is represented and entitled to provide its opinion. It also participates in the ECB’s joint supervisory team responsible for overseeing Luminor’s operations and development. At the time, the Bank of Latvia explained that the ECB directly supervised Latvia’s three largest banks by assets—Swedbank, SEB banka and Citadele—while in Estonia it supervised four major institutions: Swedbank, SEB Pank, Luminor Bank and LHV Pank. In May 2024, then Speaker of the Lithuanian Parliament Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen urged caution regarding the proposed acquisition, pointing to Hungary’s position on Ukraine and Russia, which she said differed significantly from the broader consensus within the European Union. According to Luminor, the bank is the third-largest financial services provider in the Baltic states, serving private individuals, families and businesses. In 2025, Luminor reported a net profit of 158 million euros and a return on equity of 8.6%. At the end of the year, its Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio stood at 20.2%, while its total capital adequacy ratio reached 24.6%. Luminor operates in Latvia through a local branch, which is the country’s fourth-largest bank by assets. Prior to the announced transaction, the bank was controlled by investment funds managed by Blackstone. Europe’s Bold Move Against Google Raises Bigger Questions by Sir Democracy Community This content is not subject to review by Daily Kos staff prior to publication. July 25, 2026 at 2:23 PM Recommend Story Share: Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share using Native tools Share Copied to clipboard 10 Comments Add Daily Kos to Google Synopsis Synopsis (Gen Z Version) What happens when one of the world’s most powerful tech companies collides with one of the world’s toughest regulators? That’s exactly what’s unfolding in Brussels, where the European Commission has taken major action against Alphabet, the parent company of Google, led by CEO Sundar Pichai. For most of us, Google is simply part of daily life—a search engine we’ve used for years without giving it much thought. But behind every search result lies a company so influential that governments on both sides of the Atlantic are debating just how much power it should have. In this article, I’ll break down how European regulators arrived at their decision after years of investigations and oversight, and why they believe Big Tech needs stronger rules. I’ll also examine the reaction from Alphabet executives, who argue that the EU’s approach could hurt innovation, investment, and consumer choice. But this story goes far beyond Google. The dispute is quickly becoming part of a much larger clash between Europe and the United States. Since President Donald Trump returned to the White House for a second, nonconsecutive term, tensions between Washington and Brussels have grown more visible. Trade disagreements, technology regulation, and competing economic interests are increasingly pushing both sides toward confrontation rather than cooperation. And the stakes may be about to get even higher. The Trump Administration has signaled that it could impose tariffs exceeding those announced during the so-called “Liberation Day” trade measures of April 2, 2025. If that happens, European leaders could respond aggressively—potentially tearing up the trade agreement reached when Trump met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Scotland. Economists have long warned about the possibility of a full-scale transatlantic trade war. While those fears eased after the tensions surrounding Liberation Day, they may not stay buried for long. If Washington raises tariffs on European goods and Brussels retaliates with its own tariffs—what some officials call deploying the EU’s “trade bazooka”—the conflict could escalate rapidly. By the end of this article, I want readers to think about a bigger question: Is this really just a fight over Google, or is it a sign that the U.S. and Europe are entering a new era of economic rivalry? What happens next could reshape not only the future of Big Tech, but also the future of one of the world’s most important international relationships: NATO. What took Van der Leyen so long? One of the most common questions people ask is: If European regulators believed companies like Google were abusing their market power, why did it take so many years to act? The European Commission couldn’t simply decide overnight to impose a massive fine; it had to build a legally sound case capable of withstanding years of appeals from some of the world’s wealthiest and most formidable legal teams. At the same time, the Commission remained acutely aware of public scrutiny—any further delay risked testing the electorate’s patience and potentially weakening Van der Leyen’s position as EU Commission President and leader of the-right European People’s Party (E.P.P). This, in turn, could make it even more challenging for her party’s next nominee to secure support from both left- and right-leaning MEPs. Author’s Note: For context, not so very long ago, Van der Leyen had a rough time getting re-elected—some MEPs weren’t feeling her, so she had to make some unpopular moves to win them over. With the EU Parliament so divided between left and right, it makes sense that she took her time before acting on Google if she thought they broke the DMA rules. 1. Big Tech Is Complicated Unlike a traditional monopoly case involving railroads, oil companies, or banks, digital platforms operate in highly complex markets. Google isn’t just a search engine. It is part of a vast ecosystem that includes: Search Online advertising Mobile operating systems (Android) Web browsers (Chrome) Maps Cloud computing Artificial intelligence European regulators first had to determine whether Google’s dominance in one area gave it an unfair advantage in another. Proving that requires enormous amounts of data, economic analysis, and internal company documents. 2. The EU Wanted Evidence, Not Headlines European competition law requires regulators to demonstrate that a company has abused a dominant market position—not merely that it is successful. That process can involve: Investigating complaints from competitors. Gathering evidence across multiple countries. Interviewing businesses and consumers. Reviewing millions of pages of documents. Allowing the company being investigated to defend itself. Because Google’s services are used by hundreds of millions of Europeans, regulators had to move carefully to avoid unintended consequences that could affect consumers and businesses alike. 3. Big Tech Fights Back Another reason these cases take years is that companies rarely accept regulatory findings without a fight. Alphabet has some of the most sophisticated legal teams in the world. When Brussels issues a major decision, the company can challenge it in European courts, often leading to years of litigation. European officials know this in advance. As a result, they spend years building a case strong enough to survive judicial scrutiny. A weak case could be overturned, creating an embarrassing defeat for regulators and setting a precedent that weakens future enforcement. 4. The Rules Were Still Evolving For much of the 2000s and 2010s, lawmakers around the world struggled to figure out how to regulate digital platforms. When Google emerged as a dominant force, there were few laws specifically designed for: Search engines App stores Digital advertising platforms Algorithmic gatekeepers In many ways, governments were trying to regulate twenty-first-century technology using twentieth-century legal frameworks. That began to change when the EU introduced new legislation such as the Digital Markets Act (DMA) and the Digital Services Act (DSA) , which gave regulators stronger tools and clearer legal authority to oversee large technology companies. 5. Politics Also Played a Role The EU had to balance competing concerns: Protecting competition. Maintaining good relations with the United States. Encouraging innovation and investment. Avoiding accusations of targeting successful American firms. For years, some critics argued that aggressive action against U.S. tech companies could trigger diplomatic friction. Others argued that delaying enforcement allowed dominant firms to become even more powerful. As public concern about privacy, data collection, market concentration, and platform power grew, European politicians became increasingly willing to support tougher oversight. 6. Europe Wanted to Set a Global Standard Many European policymakers saw themselves as doing more than regulating Google. They viewed these cases as part of a broader effort to answer a fundamental question: Who sets the rules for the digital economy—the world’s largest technology companies or democratically elected governments? From Brussels’ perspective, the goal was to establish the principle that even the most powerful global corporations must comply with local competition rules when operating inside the European Union. The Bigger Picture The delay was not necessarily a sign of weakness or indecision. Rather, it reflected the reality that regulators were confronting an entirely new type of economic power. Building cases against digital giants required new laws, new expertise, and years of investigation. For many European officials, the eventual fines against Alphabet and other Big Tech firms are the culmination of a long campaign to prove that no company—not even one as influential as Google—is beyond regulatory oversight. For critics, however, the years of investigations demonstrate how difficult it is for governments to keep pace with technology companies that innovate and expand far faster than regulators can write rules. That debate remains unresolved, and it is likely to shape U.S.-European relations for years or decades to come. Even after Trump leaves office in January 2029, willingly or not, I sincerely doubt the EU would be as joyful that he’s gone as they were in 2021 when Biden became president. I mean that European leaders may have mixed feelings about Trump’s departure. While some might welcome the end of his more confrontational policies, others could see opportunities or leverage in maintaining continuity, or they may remain cautious due to long-standing tensions and uncertainty about future U.S. administrations. Essentially, Europe’s reaction would likely be measured rather than openly celebratory simply because transatlantic relations may be permanently destroyed if not tainted by then. How Alphabet Reacted to the Fine Not surprisingly, Alphabet executives strongly pushed back against the nearly €900 million penalty, arguing that the European Commission’s interpretation of the Digital Markets Act could force Google to scale back popular features and make its services less useful for consumers. Company leaders portrayed the ruling as an obstacle to innovation rather than a victory for competition and signaled that they were prepared to challenge the decision through the courts. Public reaction across Europe is likely to be far more mixed. Many Europeans who favor stricter oversight of Big Tech may view the fine as a necessary step toward ensuring fair competition and preventing powerful digital platforms from abusing their market position. Others, however, may question whether such aggressive regulation could have unintended consequences. Given the deep divisions in public opinion over the role of both Big Tech and EU institutions, some critics may argue that the crackdown risks making Google’s products less convenient or effective over time—particularly if European courts ultimately uphold the Commission’s decision and require lasting changes to how the company’s services operate. The Stark Divide One of the less discussed aspects of today’s transatlantic disputes is the stark difference in how the United States and Europe developed their technology sectors. Since the rise of the internet in the late twentieth century, the United States has consistently produced many of the world’s largest and most influential technology companies. Supportive investment markets, a strong venture-capital culture, world-renowned universities, and a generally business-friendly environment helped create firms such as Google, Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, Snapchat, and countless other digital platforms that would eventually reshape the global economy. Europe, by contrast, followed a different path. While the continent excelled in manufacturing, engineering, pharmaceuticals, finance, and industrial innovation, it never produced the same number of globally dominant consumer technology giants. As a result, many of the digital tools and platforms used daily by Europeans came to be controlled by American companies rather than homegrown competitors. This imbalance emerged over several presidential administrations in Washington. During the presidency of the late George H. W. Bush (1989–1993) (died during Trump’s first term), the foundations of the commercial internet were beginning to take shape. Under Bill Clinton (1993–2001) , the internet economy exploded, helping launch many of the companies that would define the digital age. During the administrations of George W. Bush (2001–2009) and Barack Obama (2009–2017) , America’s technology sector expanded into an unprecedented global force, with Silicon Valley becoming synonymous with innovation and entrepreneurship. For much of this period, European leaders did not view America’s technological dominance as a major political challenge. That began to change when Donald Trump (2017–2021) entered the White House. Although the most visible disputes between Washington and Brussels focused on trade and NATO spending, European policymakers increasingly started debating whether the continent had become too dependent on American digital infrastructure and technology companies. Relations improved during the presidency of Joe Biden (2021–2025) , as the United States and Europe worked more closely together on issues ranging from security to technology regulation. Even so, Brussels continued developing stricter rules for large digital platforms through legislation such as the Digital Markets Act and the Digital Services Act, signaling that concerns about market concentration and technological dependence had not disappeared. Since Donald Trump’s return to office for a second, nonconsecutive term in 2025 , those concerns have become more pronounced. New tariff threats, growing trade tensions, and disputes over the regulation of major American technology companies have pushed many European officials to rethink the broader transatlantic relationship. In that context, battles involving Alphabet, Meta, Apple, Amazon, and other U.S. tech giants are increasingly being viewed not simply as competition cases, but as part of a larger debate over economic sovereignty, technological independence, and Europe’s ability to chart its own course in an increasingly competitive global economy. Big Tech, Bigger Tensions: Where Do Europe and America Go From Here? The dispute over Google’s fine is about far more than competition law. At its core, it reflects a growing disagreement between Washington and Brussels over who should set the rules for the digital economy. While European policymakers argue that large technology companies must be regulated to ensure fair competition, many American officials view these actions as disproportionately targeting successful U.S. firms. If that disagreement deepens, what begins as a regulatory dispute could eventually evolve into a much broader trade conflict. One possible flashpoint would be the use of U.S. trade laws from the 1970s that grant the President authority to impose tariffs on foreign imports under certain circumstances. President Trump has previously demonstrated a willingness to use these powers aggressively, arguing that tariffs are an effective tool for protecting American economic interests and pressuring trading partners into negotiations. Should the White House conclude that European regulations unfairly discriminate against American technology companies such as Google, Apple, Meta, Amazon, or Microsoft, it could choose to respond with tariffs on a wide range of European goods. For Brussels, such a move would likely be seen as economic coercion rather than a legitimate response to technology regulation. European leaders have repeatedly insisted that the Digital Markets Act and other competition measures apply to all companies operating within the European Union, regardless of their nationality. In their view, fines imposed on Alphabet or other American firms are enforcement actions designed to uphold European law, not attacks on the United States. If Washington nevertheless proceeded with punitive tariffs, the European Union would face pressure to respond. Initially, the response could take the form of traditional retaliatory tariffs on American exports. https://www.moneytalksnews.com/coolcatio.text: USA TODAY Network / Reuters Is the rush to the Arctic Circle really the smartest way to beat the summer heat, or is it just the fastest way to burn through your savings? The travel industry is obsessed with “coolcations” — flocking to Scandinavia, Alaska and Iceland as global temperatures rise. But many of the cool destinations have become overcrowded tourist traps. Maybe the smart move this summer is a “hotcation”: Head straight for the heat, where luxury is cheap and the air conditioning is cold. The Cold, Hard Truth About Coolcations The marketing pitch for a coolcation is simple: Escape the sweltering summer by heading north. But the reality can be a sweaty, expensive mess. Terence Leung, a marketing manager from Calgary, followed the herd to Scandinavia last July. He expected a quiet getaway but found rooms had doubled in price and ferry routes were fully booked. Worse, he ran into a heat wave in Oslo. “I was in hotels without air conditioning,” he recalled. “People started pacing the hallways at midnight, unable to sleep.” Adam Tank, a tech executive from Kansas City, had an even worse experience in Iceland. Trying to beat the late summer heat, he rented a car to drive the island’s famous ring road. After a mudslide delayed his arrival in a northern village, he got lost and asked a police officer for directions. “They said yes to my request and asked me to follow them,” said Tank. But instead of leading him to his vacation rental, the police drove him 30 minutes out of town into the middle of nowhere. “The cops clearly weren’t thrilled with the amount of tourism and didn’t want us in their town,” he said. See Also: HELOC Vs. Reverse Mortgage: Which Is Right for You? Is the ‘Coolcation’ Just a Marketing Gimmick? According to industry insiders, the coolcation trend isn’t an organic response to climate change, but a calculated move to sell inventory. “It is a classic inventory problem solved with premium branding,” said Delbert Lee, a former vice president of sales for a tour company. He explains that companies identified destinations with low summer demand and repackaged them as exclusive escapes, charging 30% to 40% more for infrastructure that was never built to handle peak crowds during the summer. Samuel Huang, CEO of an ad agency in Singapore, agrees. His firm has been tracking worldwide advertising content for years, and it’s seen a 30% to 40% increase in ad spend targeting warmer regions with arctic imagery. “This marketing push creates an artificial scarcity that inflates prices for subpar infrastructure,” Huang said. He noted that negative online reviews for these destinations are climbing by 30% quarter-over-quarter. Lorena Basualdo, a luxury travel adviser who specializes in Italian vacations, pointed out that northern gateways have brief summers and limited transport slots. “You’ll still find limited AC, small elevators, scarce shade structures, undersized water stations, and transit timetables that can’t stretch during surges,” she warned. The Case for the ‘Hotcation’ While everyone else is fighting for a view of a glacier, the “hotcation” — embracing the heat in places like Phoenix, Dubai or Madrid — is emerging as a value play. “A luxury hotel in Dubai or Phoenix operates at a loss during its summer off-season,” explains Lee. He said these properties offer 50% to 70% discounts not as a special deal, but as a baseline necessity. Amanda Persi, CEO of The Getaway Co., agrees that hot destinations can offer better value, but warns that travelers must be honest with themselves about the heat. “Sightseeing all day in the sun isn’t always realistic,” Persi said. She notes that if you treat the trip less like a checklist and more like a lifestyle — slowing down and resting by the pool during the day — the experience can be magical. Leung, who felt burned by his Scandinavian adventure, eventually tried this approach. “During peak heat, Phoenix and Madrid were empty and cheap,” he said. The resorts had shaded areas, ice-cold air and open pools. “Heat can be managed,” he added. “Scarcity and crowds can’t.” I’ve spent a few summers in hot-weather destinations like Phoenix and the Florida Keys, and I’m with Leung on this one. The tourists leave, and the rates drop faster than the temperature in your air-conditioned hotel room. But Is It a Fair Comparison? Of course, not everyone agrees that swapping a glacier for a desert pool is a valid comparison. Jared Sternberg, founder of Gondwana Ecotours, argues that comparing Alaska to Phoenix is meaningless. “One is about immersion in wild landscapes, long daylight, wildlife and remoteness; the other is about urban comfort,” Sternberg said. Experts also defend the high prices of remote destinations. Sternberg notes that Alaska faces significantly higher infrastructure costs and shorter operating seasons. Andrew Harrison, a travel advisor with OvationNetwork, points out that the high price tags in Scandinavia reflect the reality of the local economy. “Scandinavia has the highest fuel and labor costs in the world, and the prices for the trip reflect that,” Harrison said. Travelers Are Voting With Their Wallets Despite the warnings, it looks like travelers are trending toward hotcations this summer. Lauren McCormick, a spokeswoman for the travel insurance company Squaremouth, said interest in hot-weather destinations for this summer has outpaced demand for cool-weather getaways. Squaremouth’s data shows interest in Costa Rica has jumped nearly 41% and Italy is up 24%, while searches for Norway have dropped by nearly 18%. Still, she warned that a hotcation comes with risks. “Hot destinations, especially during summer months, bring added health and safety considerations, such as heat-related illnesses,” she said. McCormick recommended either travel insurance or medical insurance with at least $50,000 in medical coverage and $100,000 for medical evacuation. How to Travel Smarter This Summer If you want to avoid the “coolcation” trap but aren’t ready to bake in the desert, there are middle-ground solutions. Wait for the shoulder season. Mitch Krayton, a Denver travel agent, warns against the Arctic or Alaska in high summer. “Go in the shoulder season or offseason to avoid the crowds and get the best rates,” he said. For Alaska, that means September and October. Look for alternative cool spots. Sam Bruce, co-founder of Much Better Adventures, suggests looking at cooler places outside the obvious circuit, like Estonia, where you can enjoy milder summers without the overcrowding. Check the AC. Don’t assume a northern hotel is equipped for a heat wave. Basualdo said you must ensure your room has an air conditioner. “Filter out the ones that don’t,” she said. So this summer, you might not want to hang out with the cool kids heading north with the herd. They’re putting a strain on the infrastructure, and ironically, they may suffer through a heat wave without air conditioning. Ultimately, the hottest summer destination might literally be the hottest summer destination. Christopher Elliott is an author, consumer advocate and journalist. He founded Elliott Advocacy, a nonprofit organization that helps solve consumer problems. He publishes Elliott Confidential, a travel newsletter, and the Elliott Report, a news site about customer service.
